item.title: From IBD tracts to runs of homozygosity: a unified coalescent framework including selection
item.description: arXiv:2605.03498v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) tracts and runs of homozygosity (ROH) represent the underlying and observable aspects of chromosomal autozygosity, but no formal relationship between them had been established. This study develops a coalescent framework that connects these concepts, providing tools for detecting selection signatures and extending the temporal range of effective population size (Ne) inference. Closed-form probability functions are derived for IBD tract lengths and mapped onto observable ROHs by modelling the displacement of autozygosity boundaries from true recombination breakpoints to the nearest heterozygous marker. This mapping explicitly accounts for mutation, gene conversion, marker density, and heterozygosity. Selection effects are incorporated analytically, yielding computational tools to predict tract length distributions under background selection and partial or complete selective sweeps. Background selection shifts IBD tract-length distributions toward longer tracts, an effect better explained by a generation-dependent Ne reduction below its neutral value than by a single constant Ne. Selective sweeps generate directional asymmetry in tract-length distributions at neutral sites linked with the selected locus, with its direction indicating on which side of the neutral site the selected locus resides. This asymmetry decays rapidly after the sweep, whereas the local Ne reduction estimated from the median tract length persists considerably longer. The coalescent framework is further extended to arbitrary time-varying population size, enabling insights into past demography across a wide temporal range.
item.dc:creator: Enrique Santiago

item.title: Mutant Fixation for a Stochastic Evolutionary Model in Fragmented Populations
item.description: arXiv:2606.23946v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Population fragmentation is a common feature of many biological systems. Understanding mutant fixation in such systems is challenging because the underlying stochastic dynamics are high-dimensional. In this work, we develop a general mathematical framework for analyzing stochastic evolution in fragmented populations connected by rare migration. The framework is sufficiently general to accommodate heterogeneous deme sizes, deme-dependent birth and death processes, and migration on arbitrary strongly connected directed networks with asymmetric migration rates. We show that, in the limit where migration occurs on a much slower timescale than within-deme dynamics, the full stochastic process can be reduced to a lower-dimensional Markov chain whose states correspond to configurations of fully mutant and fully wild-type demes. The reduction theorem establishes that fixation probabilities and absorption times of the original process are asymptotically determined by the corresponding quantities of a reduced chain. As an application, we derive explicit formulas for mutant fixation probabilities and fixation times in fragmented populations initiated by the introduction of a single mutant. The results provide a general and tractable approach for studying evolutionary dynamics in complex fragmented populations.
item.dc:creator: Yi Fu, Natalia L. Komarova

item.title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
item.description: arXiv:2610.30776v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost. On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves; the single-exponential dependence on K is tight under ETH, already with every leaf observed. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources. We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it, at every error tolerance. Which references are missing then matters far more than how many. Under nearest-to-source deletion a median of two references can be erased before the generating support stops being the unique smallest explanation, and that budget stays nearly flat as the panel grows (Spearman 0.10 over 20 to 361 references, against 0.82 for random loss). Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%. That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. The generating configuration's worst-leaf residual exceeds the one-source optimum in all 296 real ANI cases, and in 248 after refitting the common pendant. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. A point estimate of the count alone does not quantify it. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Tang

item.title: Short-wave signal versus indirect prey-taxis
item.description: arXiv:2604.20469v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address a short-wave asymptotic for one class of quasi-linear second-order PDE systems involving the cross-diffusion described by the so-called Patlak-Keller-Segel law. It is common to employ these equations for modeling the predator-prey community with the prey-taxis, which means the interactions of two species of particles or cells or anything else through which the species called "predators" is capable of moving directionally while searching for the other species called "prey." However, we suppose the predators to be sensitive not to the prey density but to a cue produced by the prey. Additionally, the production of the cue is assumed to be sensitive to the intensity of an external field, which is independent of the community state. This is what we call the external signal. It can be due to the spatiotemporal inhomogeneity of the environment arising from natural or artificial reasons. We assume that the external signal takes a general short-wave form and construct a complete formal asymptotic expansion for the short-wave solutions (modulo solving a chain of the so-called slow systems) with no restrictions on the spatial dimension or kinetics of inter- or intra-specific reactions. Further, we apply the short-wave asymptotic to studying the stability or instability induced by the external signal following Kapitza's theory for the upside-down pendulum. Applying the general results to some special classes of external signals, we get examples of suppressing the taxical transport, examples of the robustness of the species equilibrium to the signal up to a very strong stabilization or, oppositely, destabilization, and something like blurring the borderline in the parametric space between the areas of stability and instability of this equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Morgulis, Karrar Malal

item.title: A method for including additional socio-demographic factors in social contact matrices for compartment-based epidemic models
item.description: arXiv:2605.13870v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Socio-demographic factors influence social contact patterns and play a fundamental role in shaping the transmission dynamics of infectious diseases. However, compartment-based models of infectious disease dynamics commonly consider the dependence of contact patterns on age, but ignore other factors that are likely to have compounding effects. Methods that stratify the population by multiple socio-demographic factors are few and require social contact surveys that contain information about all factors of interest. Here we present a method that can stratify an existing social contact matrix with an additional socio-demographic factor using information about the population structure of the socio-demographic factors and assumptions about the aggregate mixing rates within and between groups. We then analyse hypothetical populations and a projection of a social contact survey onto Aotearoa New Zealand's age-ethnic structure to show how these extended social contact matrices can change epidemic dynamics and outcomes. The inclusion of the additional factor has a big impact on the model reproduction number and final epidemic size. We find that minority group epidemic outcomes are most sensitive to variation in model parameter values.
item.dc:creator: Vincent X. Lomas, Tim Chambers, Leighton Watson, Michael Plank

item.title: A Framework for Evaluating Forward Contamination Risk for Bio-ISRU Microorganisms
item.description: arXiv:2609.12015v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: NASA planetary protection policy seeks to avoid inadvertent forward contamination of celestial bodies and backward contamination of Earth during space exploration. For Mars missions, it has historically focused on sterilization of landers and rovers. Current policy provides no framework for assessing the forward contamination risk of missions that deliberately include living organisms and must not be sterilized, such as a human crew, agriculture, or biotechnology for manufacturing and life support. We propose the PRIM (Propagation Restricted, Inert on Mars) framework to evaluate the forward-contamination risk posed by known organisms. Building on the biocontainment literature and probability-of-contamination model, PRIM bounds the ability of an organism released from a worst-case off-nominal event to sustain growth on the Martian surface at a probability under P_c <= 10^-4 using independent single-stressor propagation assays. We apply the PRIM framework to two engineered Mars biological in situ resource utilization chassis organisms, using low water activity and carbon starvation to qualify them for low forward contamination risk even at high bioburden, and outline how to extend the assays to phototrophs and anaerobes. PRIM offers a path to flight-qualify living organisms for Mars based on laboratory assays rather than bioburden alone. This enables biological life support infrastructure for a sustained presence on Mars while keeping forward contamination risk demonstrably low.
item.dc:creator: Una Nattermann, Devon A. Stork, Tom Pedersen, Nathan D. Hicks, Jordan E. Mancuso, Keren Isaev, Max G. Schubert, Fatima R. Martin, Jonathan Liu, Harley Greene, Edward Sukarto, Erika A. DeBenedictis

item.title: Asymptotics and finite sample bounds for prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher hidden Markov models
item.description: arXiv:2609.22444v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study signal prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models whose latent signal is a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion and whose discrete-time observations are categorical. We consider a repeated-sampling regime with finitely many inspection times and large within-time samples. Under neutrality and parent-independent mutation, the Bayesian predictive and smoothing laws admit exact representations as mixtures of Dirichlet distributions. We show that the one-step predictive and local smoothing laws converge in total variation to the corresponding Wright-Fisher transition and bridge laws determined by the neighboring population frequencies, thereby justifying plug-in approximations based on empirical proportions. For prediction, we derive explicit finite-sample bounds for this approximation and for bounded predictive functionals such as diversity, together with a finite-sample concentration bound for the marginal smoother. The joint posterior at the inspection times concentrates at the target frequencies and satisfies a Bernstein-von Mises limit with distinct interior and boundary regimes, with Gaussian and Gamma limits on different scales. The results allow arbitrary dependence across inspection times. A key technical ingredient is a fixed-interval tail bound for the coalescent-based dual death process.
item.dc:creator: Luigi M. Malgieri, Filippo Ascolani, Matteo Giordano, Matteo Ruggiero
